title: the serpent-arrows and Garuda
hook: why the snakes run from Garuda, and why Garuda would come to Rama

segments.voice: Yesterday: Garuda. A great wind, the snakes let go, a touch on the face, and your line, I'm your friend, don't ask why. Did you let some air move around you? Today, the why, and the week closes. Day six hundred forty-four.

The arrows that were snakes didn't fight Garuda. The moment his wind reached the shore, they let go and fled. People who grew up with Indian tales know exactly why. They've heard it from grandparents, in comics, in temple carvings. It's a story about two sisters, a horse's tail, a cheat, and a son who will do anything to set his mother free. Valmiki doesn't stop to tell it. Today we will.
screen: `THE SNAKES DON'T FIGHT. THEY FLEE.` → `TWO SISTERS AND A HORSE'S TAIL.` → `A SON WHO FREES HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Mahabharata's first book. Two sisters, Kadru and Vinata, are both wives of the sage Kashyapa. Kadru is the mother of the serpents. Vinata is the mother of Garuda. The sisters make a bet about the color of a divine horse's tail, and the loser becomes the winner's servant. Kadru cheats: she has her serpent sons hang on the tail so it looks black. Vinata loses, and becomes a servant to her sister and the snakes. Her son Garuda asks the serpents: what will it take to free my mother? Bring us the nectar of immortality, they say, from the gods. So Garuda storms heaven, wins the nectar, and frees his mother. On the way, Vishnu meets him and offers him a gift, and Garuda in turn agrees to serve Vishnu, as the bird he rides and the emblem on his banner. That's why snakes and Garuda are enemies, and why Garuda is Vishnu's own carrier. Now put that back on the battlefield at Lanka. The bird who carries Vishnu comes down to free Rama, calls himself his friend, and won't say why. For many Hindus that's a quiet sign of who Rama is: Vishnu come to earth. Valmiki doesn't spell it out here. He lets the reader notice. And that closes a week that went from Vibhishana welcomed on the beach, to spies set free, to a last offer at the gates, to arrows from the sky, and a friend on the wind.
screen: `KADRU AND VINATA.` · `THE CHEAT ON THE HORSE'S TAIL.` · `GARUDA FREES HIS MOTHER.` · `THE BIRD WHO CARRIES VISHNU.` · then, large: `A WEEK FROM REFUGE TO RESCUE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath slow. Think of someone in your life who, like Garuda, would cross anything for a person they love: a parent, a friend, a sibling, maybe you. Picture them. Notice what that kind of loyalty feels like from the outside. Then let the picture go, and rest in the breath. Seven days, one week of the war, come to a close. The bell holds the time.
Garuda, the great bird, old enemy of serpents since he freed his mother from Kadru's serpents. He carries Vishnu, and comes down to free Rama.
Your line: a friend on the wind. Today, think of one person who'd cross anything for someone they love, and thank them if you can. Day six hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Garuda's story from the Mahabharata's Adi Parva is often told to children, and in many Vishnu temples a figure of Garuda faces the main shrine with folded hands.

fork.setup: you're Garuda. your mother is a servant because of a cheat. the serpents name their price: the gods' nectar. what do you do?
options: storm heaven and bring the nectar.
fork.reveal: he wins the nectar from the gods, frees his mother, and on the way agrees to serve Vishnu.

original.note: Sanskrit amṛta: the nectar of immortality, literally 'not dying', from a-, not, and mṛta, dead.

trapdoor: what you thought: snakes and eagles just don't get along.
what it means: Garuda's enmity with the serpents goes back to his mother's servitude to Kadru and her sons.
what a scholar hears: the Garuda story is told in the Mahabharata's Adi Parva, in the section often called the Astika Parva.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Astika Parva: Kadru and Vinata; Garuda wins the nectar and becomes Vishnu's carrier)

notes: The Kadru–Vinata story is summarized from the Mahabharata, Adi Parva (chapters around 14–30 in the vulgate); confirm the details used (the horse Uccaiḥśravas, the tail made to look black, the nectar as ransom).
Garuda becoming Vishnu's carrier and banner emblem in exchange for a boon: confirm.
The statement that many Hindus read Garuda's arrival as a sign of Rama's divinity is framed as a reading, not as Valmiki's explicit claim.
